name: whole-school-upright-piano
idea: The whole primary school sings it: a hall of two hundred children aged 5 to 11 in rough unison, not a trained choir, slightly behind the beat and a touch flat, a few voices louder than the rest, recorded from the back of a wooden-floored school hall. The accompaniment is an out-of-tune upright school piano played firmly by one teacher, thumping block chords in a plain common-metre hymn tune at a steady marching walk (about 80 bpm). Ask for the sound by describing the room and the event (1980s British primary school assembly, Come and Praise era) rather than by genre words, and keep it to one four-line verse after two bars of piano introduction. It ends on the last word: one held piano chord, then silence, no fade, no second verse.

name: solo-cathedral-treble
idea: One trained boy treble, a cathedral chorister of about eleven, sings all four lines alone: pure, vibrato-free, very English, every consonant clean, utterly sincere about every word. Behind him a large pipe organ in a stone cathedral holds soft sustained chords on quiet flute stops, swelling only slightly on the third line, with a long natural stone reverb. Ask for it as Anglican choral music (evensong, solo treble with organ), state that the voice is a child, and exclude adult soprano, female vocals, operatic vibrato and pop. Slow and grave (about 60 bpm), the beauty played completely straight; the organ resolves under the last word and the reverb dies away to silence.

name: one-small-girl-nervous
idea: A single untrained girl of about seven, picked to sing in front of the assembly, sings the four lines alone: small, breathy, close to the microphone, a little hesitant, slightly off pitch on the high notes, but carrying the tune bravely. Under her a church chamber organ plays the hymn very quietly on one soft stop, simple four-part chords that follow her rather than lead, slowing when she slows. Ask for it as an intimate, dry, almost documentary recording, a child's solo at a school service, and exclude choir, polished vocals, reverb-heavy production, drums and strings. The organ lifts off after her last word and there is nothing after it.

name: edwardian-sunday-school-78
idea: A Sunday-school children's choir recorded around 1910 on a shellac 78 record: twenty children singing in unison with crisp Edwardian diction, accompanied by a wheezing pedal harmonium pumped a little unevenly. Ask for the music through its period and its recording: acoustic-era horn recording, narrow mid-range, surface crackle and hiss, slight speed wobble, no bass, no modern production. A brisk, upright Victorian hymn tune in common metre (about 92 bpm), sung with cheerful moral certainty as if it were a lesson in good conduct. Three harmonium chords as an introduction, the four lines once, a final amen-style cadence on the last word, then only the crackle of the run-out groove.
